scpParadigm.description: Structure‑Conduct‑Performance paradigm: market structure affects firm conduct (pricing, R&D, collusion) which affects performance (profitability, efficiency).
scpParadigm.criticism: Endogeneity concerns: unobserved demand/supply shocks affect both structure and performance; efficiency differences may drive concentration.

boundsApproach.description: Sutton's bounds approach: identifies strong mechanisms that bound market outcomes across industries without full specification. Entry is endogenous; equilibrium must satisfy stability and viability.
keyFindings: When advertising/R&D are less important, lower bound on concentration falls as market size grows.
When advertising/R&D are more important, concentration is bounded below (largest firm share remains positive).
Intensified price competition shifts lower bound of concentration upward.
boundsApproach.policyImplication: Pro‑competition regulations may lead to more concentrated markets (exit/consolidation).

conductParameter.description: Estimates a conduct parameter (conjectural variations) to measure market power, using demand‑supply systems.
conductParameter.identification: Requires rotation of demand curve (interaction term) to separate marginal cost from conduct.
conductParameter.criticism: Static models may mis‑measure market power (Corts critique); dynamic extensions handle strategic/fundamental reasons.

dynamicFactors.fundamental: stock variables (capital, resources) affect future profits
dynamicFactors.strategic: beliefs about rivals' responses to current actions

conductParameter.fullMarginalCost: P = MC + γ·λ (shadow value of constraints)

productDifferentiation.vertical: All consumers agree on quality ranking.

schumpeter.keyInsight: Capitalism is dynamic; perfect competition stifles innovation because free entry erodes incentives.
schumpeter.criticism: Market power may foster innovation due to large scale and ability to capture rents.

arrow1962.drastic: new technology price < old MC; monopolist remains monopolist.
arrow1962.nonDrastic: competitive firm's incentive can be lower because it cannot price above competitive price.
arrow1962.result: Competitive firm has greater incentive to innovate (replacement effect).

gilbertNewbery1982.result: Incumbent may pre‑empt entry by patenting (preemption) if monopoly profit exceeds post‑entry industry profit.

reinganum1983.result: With stochastic innovation (Poisson), challenger has greater incentive than incumbent (no replacement effect), overturning Gilbert‑Newbery.

kamienSchwartz1976.result: Relationship between rivalry (hazard rate) and innovation timing is U‑shaped for large innovation, positive for small innovation.

aghionEtAl2001.description: Step‑by‑step innovation; neck‑and‑neck vs unleveled sectors.
aghionEtAl2001.result: Large innovation leads to inverted‑U (competition‑innovation) due to escape‑competition effect vs Schumpeterian effect.

hashmi2013.result: Relationship depends on technology gap: small gap → increasing; intermediate → inverted‑U; large gap → decreasing.

empiricalFindings.linear: Nickell (1996), Blundell et al. (1999) find positive relationship.
empiricalFindings.nonLinear: Mixed: ABBGH find inverted‑U; Correa and Ornaghi find positive; Hashmi finds weakly negative.
empiricalFindings.naturalExperiments: Holmes & Schmitz (railroads, iron ore) show competition boosts productivity.
